definitions.definition: A research program that looks for patterns that are the same in physics, theology, information theory, and consciousness.
definitions.example: Like finding that the same shape appears in a snowflake, a crystal, and a math formula.

definitions.definition: When two different systems have the same underlying structure or pattern, even if they look different on the surface.
definitions.example: A map of a subway system and a map of a computer network can have the same structure even though one is trains and the other is data.

definitions.definition: A word meaning 'three-in-one,' used to describe God as three persons (Father, Son, Holy Spirit) but one being.
definitions.example: Like how water can be ice, liquid, and steam but is still H2O.

definitions.definition: The part of Christian theology that studies how people are saved, specifically from the Reformed (Calvinist) tradition.
definitions.example: It's the study of salvation according to the beliefs of churches that follow John Calvin.

definitions.definition: The belief that mathematical truths are real and exist whether or not anyone is thinking about them.
definitions.example: The fact that 2+2=4 was true even before humans existed.

definitions.definition: A method of studying how the same patterns show up in different fields of knowledge.
definitions.example: Looking at how the idea of a 'network' appears in social media, the brain, and the internet.

definitions.definition: Specific tests that could prove a theory wrong, so you know when to abandon it.
definitions.example: If you claim all swans are white, a kill condition is seeing a black swan.

definitions.definition: A clear statement of what evidence would prove a claim false.
definitions.example: If I say 'it rains every Tuesday,' the falsification target is a Tuesday without rain.

definitions.definition: A process where someone tries to find flaws in your argument to make it stronger.
definitions.example: Like a friend who points out holes in your plan before you try it.

definitions.definition: A proof that shows what mathematics can and cannot do, setting limits on its power.
definitions.example: Like proving that you can't use a ruler and compass to draw a square with the same area as a circle.
definitions.first_appearance: Section I - What I Do Not Claim

definitions.definition: An argument based on the shape or pattern of ideas, not just on facts.
definitions.example: Saying a bicycle and a unicycle are similar because both have wheels, even though one has two and the other has one.
definitions.first_appearance: Section I - What I Do Not Claim

definitions.definition: The idea that you must be open about your starting beliefs, because they affect everything you conclude.
definitions.example: If you start by assuming only matter exists, you can't later pretend to be neutral about spiritual things.
definitions.first_appearance: Section I - The Epistemological Honesty Principle

definitions.definition: Someone who believes that only physical matter exists, and nothing spiritual or mental is real.
definitions.example: A materialist would say your thoughts are just brain chemicals, not a soul.
definitions.first_appearance: Section I - The Epistemological Honesty Principle

definitions.definition: The branch of philosophy that asks what is real, what exists, and what is the nature of reality.
definitions.example: Questions like 'Does God exist?' or 'What is time?' are metaphysical.
definitions.first_appearance: Section I - The Epistemological Honesty Principle

definitions.definition: A Greek word (pronounced AR-kay) meaning 'beginning,' 'origin,' or 'first principle.'
definitions.example: In the Bible, 'In the beginning (arche) was the Word.'

definitions.definition: The underlying substance or material that something else is built on or happens in.
definitions.example: Soil is the substrate for a garden; a computer's hardware is the substrate for its software.

definitions.definition: Something that exists because of itself, not because of anything else.
definitions.example: If God is self-grounding, He doesn't need a creator; He just is.

definitions.definition: Stands for 'Logos-Logic Coherence,' the core mathematical framework of Theophysics that links God (Logos) to logic and coherence.
definitions.example: It's like the operating system that connects theology and physics in this theory.

definitions.definition: A Greek letter (chi, pronounced 'kai' or 'kee') used in the LLC to represent the basic, self-existing reality from which everything comes.
definitions.example: In the framework, χ is like the raw material of existence itself.

definitions.definition: A Greek word (pronounced LOH-gos) meaning 'word,' 'reason,' or 'logic.' In Christian theology, it refers to Jesus Christ as the divine reason that created and orders the universe.
definitions.example: When John says 'the Word (Logos) was God,' he means Jesus is the logic behind all creation.

definitions.definition: A mathematical formula that produces a sequence of numbers or patterns when you plug in different values.
definitions.example: Like a recipe that tells you how to make the next number in a pattern, such as 1, 2, 4, 8, 16...

definitions.definition: A mathematical expression in the LLC that describes how everything holds together in a unified, orderly way.
definitions.example: Like a formula that calculates how well a team works together versus falling apart.

definitions.definition: A Latin word (pronounced fil-ee-OH-kway) meaning 'and the Son.' It refers to the belief that the Holy Spirit comes from both the Father and the Son.
definitions.example: It's a technical term in church history about how the three persons of the Trinity relate.

definitions.definition: A mathematical way to measure how fast something changes over time.
definitions.example: If your speed is 60 mph, the time derivative of your position is 60 miles per hour.

definitions.definition: The end point or final goal of a process or journey.
definitions.example: The terminus of a bus route is the last stop.

definitions.definition: The fundamental nature or core quality that makes something what it is.
definitions.example: The essence of water is being H2O, whether it's ice, liquid, or steam.
definitions.first_appearance: Section II - One Essence, Three Persons

definitions.definition: The way the three persons of the Trinity are distinguished by how they come from each other: the Father is unbegotten (not from anyone), the Son is begotten (from the Father), and the Spirit proceeds (from the Father and Son).
definitions.example: It's like saying the difference between a parent, a child, and a breath is how they relate to each other.
definitions.first_appearance: Section II - One Essence, Three Persons

definitions.definition: The idea that many different things can be part of one whole without losing their differences.
definitions.example: A sports team has many players with different roles, but they are one team.
definitions.first_appearance: Section II - One Essence, Three Persons

definitions.definition: A mathematical system in Theophysics that uses plus and minus signs to represent grace and sin, showing how they interact.
definitions.example: Like using +1 for 'good' and -1 for 'bad' and seeing what happens when you combine them.

definitions.definition: Five key beliefs from the Protestant Reformation: grace alone, faith alone, Christ alone, Scripture alone, glory to God alone.
definitions.example: They are like the five core rules of the Reformation movement.

definitions.definition: A symbol or function that tells you to do something to a number or state, like a command in math.
definitions.example: The plus sign (+) is an operator that tells you to add; a 'grace operator' would be a command that applies grace.

definitions.definition: A symbol called the 'Grace Operator' in Theophysics, representing God's action of saving someone.
definitions.example: It's like a button that, when pressed, changes a person from lost to saved.

definitions.definition: A property where doing something twice gives the same result as doing it once.
definitions.example: If you press 'on' on a light switch that's already on, nothing changes; that's idempotent.

definitions.definition: A property of a mathematical operation that changes the size or nature of something, not just its position or angle.
definitions.example: If you stretch a rubber band, that's non-unitary because it changes length; just rotating it is unitary.

definitions.definition: A theorem in Theophysics stating that you cannot change your own spiritual state from bad to good by your own efforts.
definitions.example: It's like saying you can't lift yourself off the ground by pulling on your own shoelaces.

definitions.definition: When two operations can be done in any order and still give the same result.
definitions.example: Addition commutes because 2+3 = 3+2; subtraction does not because 5-3 ≠ 3-5.

definitions.definition: Mathematical operations that rotate or change something without changing its size or total amount.
definitions.example: Spinning a basketball in your hand is a unitary operation; squishing it is not.

definitions.definition: A code name for the 'Sign Operator Isomorphism,' a specific confirmed link between quantum mechanics and the theology of salvation in Theophysics.
definitions.example: It's like a patent number for a discovered connection between physics and faith.

definitions.definition: A one-to-one mapping between two structures that preserves their relationships, meaning they are essentially the same shape.
definitions.example: A map of a city's streets and the actual streets are isomorphic because every street on the map matches a real street.

definitions.definition: The study of salvation, or how people are saved from sin and its consequences.
definitions.example: It's the part of theology that asks 'How does someone get to heaven?'
